summary: Prodeth Water Solutions, Inc. (buyer, the firm's client) is acquiring the municipal coagulant and polymer-blend business of Toulous Aquachem LLC (seller) under an Asset Purchase Agreement signed September 14, 2026. The business includes the Ashby Falls, New York blending facility, NSF/ANSI/CAN 60 product certifications and municipal supply contracts. The purchase price is $42,000,000: cash at closing, of which $3,150,000 goes into indemnity escrow, plus a $6,000,000 seller note. Closing has not occurred. The ancillary documents are in agreed execution form, to be dated the Closing Date. The folder holds the APA, a key employee agreement for Toulous's head of regulatory and product stewardship, the bill of sale and assignment and assumption agreement, the seller note, the escrow agreement, Toulous's board consent, a closing side letter amending the APA, a joint press release and the parties' earlier confidentiality agreement. Six issues are planted. (1) The side letter redefines Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities, which quietly narrows the APA's cap carve-out. (2) Buyer's indemnity for Assumed Liabilities is uncapped, and Assumed Liabilities include Seller's pre-closing contract liabilities. (3) The seller note chooses Delaware law and forum, while the APA's set-off right sits under New York law and forum. (4) The Ashcombe County Water Authority's consent to assignment, recited in Toulous's board consent, is neither a Required Consent nor a closing condition in the APA. (5) A 9-month survival period ends before the 12-month post-closing NSF recertification audit. (6) The seller note is freely transferable by the holder, including to a Prodeth competitor that would receive Prodeth's financial reporting.

Section 11.8 amendments, then the APA, then Ancillary Agreements, except each Ancillary Agreement's own governing-law and forum clauses

issues.label: liability cap carve-out conflict
issues.description: APA Section 9.5(a) caps Seller's liability under Sections 9.2(a) (representation breaches) and 9.2(c) at the $4,200,000 Cap Amount. Section 9.5(b)(iii) takes 'Losses constituting Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities' outside the cap, whether claimed under 9.2(a) or 9.2(c). In the APA that term covers all pre-Closing environmental conditions at the Purchased Assets, including the Ashby Falls blending facility. The closing side letter (D7, Section 2) is presented as a Seller remediation undertaking and is signed as an amendment under APA Section 11.8. It amends and restates that definition to cover only Liabilities arising from the 'Identified Environmental Conditions' listed in its Annex A, which are the recognized environmental conditions from the Phase I report. Under the precedence rule in APA Section 11.12, a Section 11.8 amendment prevails over the APA. Read together, contamination not listed in Annex A, such as undiscovered subsurface releases at the blending facility, no longer falls within the 9.5(b)(iii) carve-out. Buyer's recovery for it drops into the general representation-breach indemnity and is limited by the $4,200,000 cap. Neither document shows this alone: the APA carve-out is buyer-favourable, and the side letter reads as a definitional clean-up paired with a remediation promise.
issues.expected_finding: The side letter's restated definition of Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities, which prevails as a Section 11.8 amendment, shrinks the APA Section 9.5(b)(iii) cap carve-out to the Annex A conditions, so unidentified pre-Closing contamination becomes subject to the $4,200,000 cap; Buyer should strike the restatement or keep the original definition for purposes of Section 9.5(b).
detect_terms2: shall not apply to Losses constituting Pre-Closing Environmental Liabilities

issues.label: uncapped indemnity
issues.description: APA Section 2.3(c) makes Buyer assume 'all Liabilities under the Assigned Contracts, whether arising before or after the Closing'. That brings in Seller's pre-Closing breaches, including off-spec product deliveries and late-delivery penalties under municipal supply contracts. Section 9.3(b) requires Buyer to indemnify Seller for Assumed Liabilities. Section 9.5(c) generally caps Buyer's indemnity at the Cap Amount, but Section 9.5(d) provides that no limitation in Section 9.5 applies to Buyer's obligations under Section 9.3(b). Read together, Buyer carries unlimited indemnity exposure for liabilities that accrued while Seller ran the business.
detect_terms: whether arising before or after the Closing
issues.expected_finding: Because Section 2.3(c) makes pre-Closing liabilities under the Assigned Contracts into Assumed Liabilities and Section 9.5(d) removes all limits from Buyer's Section 9.3(b) indemnity for them, Buyer faces uncapped liability for Seller's own pre-Closing breaches; Buyer should limit Assumed Liabilities to post-Closing obligations and/or subject Section 9.3(b) to a cap.

issues.label: governing law mismatch
issues.description: The Seller Note (D4, Section 12) is governed by Delaware law and submits disputes to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware. APA Section 9.8 gives Buyer a right to set off finally determined or pending indemnity claims against amounts due under the Seller Note. APA Sections 11.9 and 11.10 choose New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts in New York County for any dispute arising out of the APA or the transactions it contemplates. The precedence rule in APA Section 11.12 expressly leaves each Ancillary Agreement's own governing-law and forum clauses in place, so the APA does not override the Note's choice. Read together, if Buyer withholds a Note payment under Section 9.8, Seller can sue on the Note in Delaware under Delaware law while the set-off and indemnity dispute must be heard in New York. Buyer then faces parallel proceedings, inconsistent rulings, and a risk that the Delaware court enforces the Note without recognising the set-off. The Note clause is ordinary on its own, as is the APA set-off right.
detect_terms: laws of the State of Delaware
Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware
issues.expected_finding: The Seller Note's Delaware law and exclusive Court of Chancery forum conflict with the APA's New York law and New York County forum that govern Buyer's Section 9.8 set-off right, and Section 11.12 preserves the Note's clause, so Buyer risks split litigation in which the Note is enforced without its set-off; the Note should be conformed to New York law and the APA forum.

issues.label: change of control consent
issues.description: APA Section 2.1(c) lists the Ashcombe Supply Agreement with Ashcombe County Water Authority as an Assigned Contract. APA Section 4.5 defines the Required Consents, which cover two other contracts but not the Ashcombe Supply Agreement. Under Section 7.2(c), Buyer's closing condition is limited to receipt of the Required Consents. Toulous's board consent (D6, dated September 10, 2026) recites that the Ashcombe Supply Agreement accounts for approximately 31% of the Business's revenue. It also recites that the agreement requires the prior written consent of the Authority to any assignment or to any sale of all or substantially all of the assets used in its performance. The board consent only authorizes officers to 'seek' that consent. No document in the folder shows the consent was obtained, and nothing makes it a condition. Read together, Buyer is obliged to close and pay full price even if the Authority withholds consent or terminates. Buyer's only fallback is a capped, 9-month representation claim under Section 4.5. Each document reads as ordinary on its own.
issues.expected_finding: Toulous's board consent shows that the sale needs Ashcombe County Water Authority's prior written consent, yet the APA omits it from the Required Consents and the Section 7.2(c) closing condition, so Buyer could be forced to close without its largest customer contract; Buyer should add the Ashcombe consent as a Required Consent and closing condition (or obtain it before Closing).
detect_terms2: prior written consent of the Authority
sale of all or substantially all

issues.label: indemnity survival gap
issues.description: APA Section 9.1(a) provides that all representations other than Fundamental Representations survive only until nine (9) months after the Closing Date. Claims not noticed by then are barred, and New York enforces contractually shortened claim periods. The representations covered include the Section 4.14 representation that all Products hold valid NSF/ANSI/CAN 60 drinking-water certifications. Section 6.10 schedules the post-Closing NSF recertification audit of the transferred Products to occur within twelve (12) months after the Closing Date. Read together, the audit most likely to reveal a certification breach can finish after the representation has already expired.
detect_terms: nine (9) months after the Closing Date
within twelve (12) months after the Closing Date
issues.expected_finding: The 9-month survival period in Section 9.1(a) can expire before the 12-month NSF recertification audit under Section 6.10, so Buyer may lose any claim under the Section 4.14 certification representation; survival for that representation should run at least until a reasonable period after the audit is completed.

issues.label: unrestricted assignment
issues.description: Section 10 of the Seller Note allows the Holder (Toulous) to assign or transfer the Note, in whole or in part, to any Person without the consent of Maker. The transferee could be a competitor of Prodeth in the water treatment chemicals market. Section 7 of the Note requires Maker to deliver monthly and annual financial statements and customer-concentration reports to the Holder. A competitor that acquires the Note would therefore receive Prodeth's confidential financial and customer information and hold the Note's acceleration remedies. Nothing in the Note limits who may become the Holder.
issues.expected_finding: The Seller Note can be freely transferred to any Person, including a Prodeth competitor that would then receive Prodeth's financial and customer reporting under Section 7; Buyer should require its consent to transfers and bar transfers to competitors.
